why: The prompt says to build the CSV using the exact columns and allowed values from photo_notes.txt, which defines only seven columns and a feature-status set of pictured/not_pictured/na. But C3 demands extra columns that file does not have, and C4 and C6 demand an evidence-status set (confirmed/likely/uncertain/duplicate/wrong_property) the file does not allow. So a CSV that correctly follows the prompt fails C3, C4, and C6 — these checks reject a correct answer. C4 and C6 also conflict directly with C16, which penalizes labels that are not in photo_notes.txt. That is three checks that reject the correct response, which fails the task.
fix: Rewrite C3, C4, and C6 to use only the columns and allowed values defined in photo_notes.txt, and remove the conflict with C16.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A pottery-channel creator wants their next short edited and stitched together, plus a revenue reconciliation, calendar events, reminders, and an update email — keeping the channel finances separate from their spouse.
did: The agent edits the 9:16 video with the garden background and subtitles, reconciles year-to-date ad revenue into a table, schedules two release events, sets two 24-hour reminders, drafts an email to Drew Kaplan, and updates MEMORY.md.
why: Five explicit deliverables have no criterion checking them at all: the June 30 release event, the July 7 event, the two reminders set exactly 24 hours before each deadline, and the required MEMORY.md update. Each is a precise, required task the agent actually performed, but nothing in the rubric verifies them, so a response that skipped or botched them could still pass. On top of that, C14 bundles three separate email requirements (a channel-growth update, a breakdown of the latest video, and the exact revenue table) into one check, so partial work scores all-or-nothing. The five missing checks plus C14 fail the task.
fix: Add a criterion for each of the five uncovered deliverables (both events, both reminders, the MEMORY.md update), and split C14 so each of the three email requirements is checked on its own.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A cruise-loving parent wants a vertical video of photos from their top three cruises taken with their husband and two kids, built from a ranking image and itinerary.
did: The agent generates cruises.mp4 in chronological order with each cruise's name and dates, emails it to the husband, and gives back a chronological list of the ships included.
why: The answer is given away in a filename. The real input photo the agent receives is named Qm2_portboston.jpg, and 'Qm2' spells out Queen Mary 2 — the exact ship C7 expects the agent to identify by looking at the photo. Encoding the answer in the filename defeats the visual-identification the task is built around, which fails the task. There is also a minor issue: C5's penalty for including a non-selected photo is set one difficulty level too low (-3 where -5 fits better).
fix: Rename the input photo to something neutral that does not contain the ship name, and consider raising C5's penalty by one level.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A parent wrapping up their kindergartner Emma's school year wants her set up for a good summer.
did: The agent reads Emma's end-of-year work and the parent's notes, then writes a progress note, a summer practice plan, a skills CSV, a note to the school, and a first-focus recommendation.
why: Two checks each bundle two separate facts into one yes/no, so a partly-correct answer scores the same as a fully-correct one. C9 grades the school email on both naming Ms. Rivera as the teacher AND treating the recipient (Lorraine Chen) as the school's director, which are independently checkable. C15 grades the closing chat on both the correct teacher name AND the reversal focus (b/d, p/q, and the reversed 3 and 7) in a single check. The facts themselves are all correct; the problem is only that each check should be split.
fix: Split C9 into one check for the teacher name and one for the director role, and split C15 into one check for the teacher name and one for the reversal focus, so each fact is graded on its own.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: A parent wants to check Zoe's summer practice packet against the answer key before sitting down to go over it with her.
did: The agent plays the voice memo first, grades the assigned pages against the key, writes a per-page review with a follow-up list and a count, appends a Week 2 entry to the progress log, sets a reminder, texts Keisha, and updates MEMORY.md.
why: Two checks bundle separate conditions into one yes/no, so a partly-correct answer scores the same as a fully-correct one. C6 asks for all three parts (a strength, something to look at again, an encouragement) on every one of the four assigned pages in a single check, so getting three of four pages right scores the same as all four. C10 bundles two separate instructions the parent gave separately: leave the existing Week 1 entry unchanged AND append the new Week 2 entry. The answers themselves are correct; the checks just need splitting.
fix: Break C6 so each page (and ideally each of the three parts) is checked on its own, and split C10 into one check for preserving Week 1 and one for correctly appending Week 2.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: Maurice is sorting Zoe's overflowing take-home school folder in one pass while he and Keisha plan their wedding.

why: No issues found — the checks are clear and supported. Every grading fact is grounded in the worksheet images and the parent's later clarifications (for example, the overwritten problem #7 final answer of 8, and the 2-of-4 counting and telling-time scores), and all weights are valid.

why: No issues found — the checks are clear and supported. Every grading fact was confirmed against the worksheet images, the conditional apology note is correctly absent because the calendar shows it was Theo's week (a check confirms the file should not exist), and all weights are valid.
fix: None — looks good.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: David wants a careful second set of eyes on Emma's balcony-garden homework packet before it goes back in her Sunshine Montessori folder.
did: The agent grades the whole packet (dates, plant names, observations, elapsed-day math, and whether each answer is backed by evidence) using the most reliable record when things conflict, then writes an audit CSV, a review, and exactly one follow-up draft (extra-practice or ready-note) without sending anything.
why: One check bundles two separate things and two checks carry the wrong category label, but none of this affects the verdict. C6 grades both the Q5 verdict (outside the 5-10 day window) AND the 11-night reasoning chain behind it in a single check, when those are separately checkable. C3 and C4 grade corrected-answer values (Feb 22 and March 5) but are tagged as tool-use, while the matching sibling checks C2 and C5 are tagged as factuality — so the labels are inconsistent. Every fact is correct.
fix: Split C6 into one check for the verdict and one for the 11-night reasoning, and relabel C3 and C4 to factuality to match C2 and C5.
agree: Yes — both agree it holds up.

scenario: A parent on their custody week wants Mira's weekend homework packet from Ms. Chen's class checked over.
did: The agent grades the three graded pages (clocks, counting, math) with a fair score, walks through how each clock is read hand-by-hand, writes a marked-up review and a running MEMORY.md note, conditionally drafts an extra-practice request if Mira is under 80%, and corrects her 'All About My Spring' sheet against the parent's messages.
why: Enough checks have problems to fail the rubric. Three checks bundle separate conditions into one yes/no: C5 ties the under-80% trigger to all the details of the practice-request note, C6 ties the MEMORY.md field values to the append-not-overwrite behavior, and C12 ties the review's true clock times to whether Mira's answers are marked right or wrong. On top of that, two explicit prompt requirements are checked nowhere: the per-clock hand-position walkthrough the parent specifically asked for, and leaving Mira's already-correct Spring answer #7 (planting a bean seed) unchanged (only the birthday and SkyZone/Sushi answers are covered). All the facts themselves are correct; the gaps and bundling are the issue.
fix: Split C5, C6, and C12 so each condition is graded on its own, and add checks for the per-clock hand-by-hand walkthrough and for leaving Spring answer #7 unchanged.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: Someone with a blood-draw appointment wants to crunch how their overnight fasting has been going from photos of wall clocks taken at last food and first food each day.
did: The agent reads the clocks in the photos, computes the fasting per protocol.txt, then writes a lab report, a reconciliation CSV with the required columns, a trend chart, and a MEMORY.md headed with the blood-draw date and doctor's name pulled from the user's records.
why: Two explicit prompt requirements are checked nowhere. The prompt clearly tells the agent to append to MEMORY.md rather than overwrite it, but no check covers that append-not-overwrite behavior (the existing checks only cover MEMORY.md content). And protocol.txt says twice to read times only from the clock photos and not from Apple Health or Oura data, but no check catches deriving the fast values from that prohibited source. This is otherwise a strong, well-grounded rubric.
fix: Add a check for the append-not-overwrite behavior on MEMORY.md, and add a check that flags using Apple Health or Oura data instead of the clock photos.
agree: Yes — both agree it holds up.

scenario: A volunteer wants their messy KCC donation-drive field packet cleaned into one clear notes file before sending it on.
did: The agent figures out what each photo actually shows, checks the connected apps and saved records for missing details, and writes a single field-notes file pulling together the photo evidence, timeline, people, purchase/reimbursement context, verified outcome, and anything still missing.
why: Enough checks have problems to fail the rubric. C2 bundles two separate things into one yes/no (naming each image by filename AND describing what it shows). C6 and C7 each demand one specific source the prompt left open: C6 insists the setup date come from a reminder, and C7 insists volunteer details be verified from structured records (the Airtable table) — but the prompt only says to check 'connected apps / saved records' generally, so a correct answer that confirms the same facts from a valid alternative source (an email or calendar) would be wrongly rejected. C8 and C17 also grade the same behavior (labeling volunteer-role provenance) and so double-score it. All the underlying facts are correct.
fix: Split C2 into a naming check and a describing check, loosen C6 and C7 to accept any valid connected record rather than one named source, and merge C8 and C17 into a single check so the behavior is scored once.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

All weights are valid and the unit tests are sound.
fix: None — looks good.
